title: Use of a semitendinosus tendon transplant in hernia surgery (HoTT-TAPP)
summary:
Tendon tissue has been used for decades in knee surgery for cruciate ligament injuries. Since 2018, the tendon of the semitendinosus muscle has been used in genital prolapse surgery instead of plastic meshes (HoTT operation). The surgical results are convincing, and morbidity at the donor site is low.
Hernias are successfully treated with synthetic meshes. However, these are not without controversy even in hernia surgery. Foreign body reactions and infections can occur, mesh rejection and fistula formation have been described, and rheumatologists have seen that rheumatism can be observed significantly more frequently in people with an implanted mesh. Due to the positive experience with tendon tissue in gynecology, we would also like to use the tendon tranplant tissue in hernia surgery. The tendon is cut into a mesh using a mesh Graft roller knife as useed in skin grafts. The tissue is sewn onto an absorbable mesh and, as with the conventional method, inserted into the abdominal cavity in a minimally invasive manner. The absorbable synthethic meshes dissolves completely after 12 (vicryl) to 30 (polydioxanon) weeks. What remains is the mesh made of tendon tissue. Tendon tissue does not require a blood supply. It is supplied with nutrients via diffusion. Similar to the knee joint (cruciate ligament replacement) and gynecological patients (prolapse surgery), the tissue can be expected to last a lifetime.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
capable of giving consent, presence of an inguinal, umbilical, incisional or diaphragmatic hernia requiring surgical treatment
